articles.title: “I think some people will be saved by this”: How YOSHIKI turned his crystal piano into 40 million yen ($270,000) for Japan’s earthquake victims
articles.summary: YOSHIKI, renowned composer and leader of X JAPAN, sells his crystal piano for 40 million yen ($270,000) to aid victims of the earthquake that struck the Noto Peninsula, contributing to a total of 50 million yen for disaster relief.
articles.body: Japanese musician Yoshiki raised 40 million yen, more than $270,000, by auctioning his crystal piano to support people affected by the Noto Peninsula earthquake. The sale was announced on January 9, 2024, and bidding later ran for four days before closing on January 16, according to Yoshiki's announcement. Yoshiki, the composer and leader of X JAPAN, had used the Kawai CR 40N crystal piano for recording in his Los Angeles studio and on tour. The auction was intended to help people affected by the earthquake. During his farewell to the instrument, Yoshiki said he was sad to part with a piano he considered like family, saying, “I think some people will be saved by this.”On January 4, five days before the auction announcement, Yoshiki donated 10 million yen to the Japanese Red Cross through his US-based nonprofit, Yoshiki Foundation America. The piano auction later raised another 40 million yen, bringing the total support announced for people affected by the earthquake to 50 million yen, more than $340,000. The 10 million yen was a direct cash donation, while the 40 million yen came from the piano auction. Both amounts were intended to support earthquake victims.A farewell in HollywoodThe auction announcement coincided with a career milestone. Yoshiki's handprints and footprints were unveiled at Hollywood's TCL Chinese Theatre on January 9, 2024. He became the first Japanese star to receive the honour since the tradition began nearly a century ago. He announced the piano sale at the ceremony and performed on the Kawai CR 40N, which he had used for recordings in his Los Angeles studio and on tour. Yoshiki said the earthquake had deeply affected him and that he wanted to help, as he had done in the past.Four days earlier, on January 4, he donated 10 million yen to the Japanese Red Cross through his US-based non-profit, Yoshiki Foundation America. The sale was intended to broaden that circle of assistance and, by his own admission, 100% of the earnings from both presents went to quake-affected people.What the earthquake didThe scale of the disaster explains the urgency of the fundraiser. Kyoto University's Disaster Prevention Research Institute records the Noto Peninsula earthquake at about 16:10 Japan time on January 1, 2024, with a moment magnitude of 7.5. The earthquake caused severe shaking and triggered landslides, liquefaction, fires and a tsunami. Tsunami waves reached coastal communities including Suzu.A statement issued with Yoshiki's auction announcement said that more than 1,900 people in the region remained stranded without power, food or medicine at that point. Recovery continued for months. A year-end review by Nippon.com, drawing on national and prefectural records, reported that 51,605 people had been in shelters at the peak and that all 6,882 temporary housing units planned for earthquake evacuees were completed in 2024. By December 24, 2024, the review counted 489 earthquake-related deaths, including 261 linked to evacuation and conditions in shelters. Against numbers like these, 50 million yen is one contribution among many. It shows why relief on this scale depends on large numbers of donors, and why quick fundraisers channelled through established organisations can matter in the first weeks.A record of givingThe 2024 auction followed earlier fundraising efforts documented by Yoshiki Foundation America. The foundation's official press page records a crystal piano auction after the Great East Japan Earthquake and tsunami in March 2011, along with donations and fundraising through an X JAPAN concert in 2015 and a drum set auction in 2016. The foundation has also documented charitable support following other disasters in Japan and overseas.Yoshiki Foundation America's published records also list donations of 10 million yen following the 2016 Kumamoto earthquake, the 2018 Hokkaido Iburi East earthquake and the 2019 typhoons, as well as pianos donated to schools in districts affected by the 1995 Kobe earthquake. In April 2024, Yoshiki donated another 10 million yen to the Taiwan Red Cross following an earthquake there. These historical totals are reported by the foundation itself, including on its official press page, rather than presented as independently audited figures.The Noto auction added another chapter to Yoshiki's record of disaster relief. By selling a piano he described as like family, he directed the proceeds towards people affected by the earthquake. The fundraiser combined a personal gesture with a defined relief purpose, while the scale of the disaster showed how much work remained for communities rebuilding their lives.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1973, George Harrison donated the royalties from Living in the Material World to his foundation forever; 51 years later, it recorded £573,221 in charitable spending during 2024 alone
articles.summary: More than 50 years after George Harrison promised to donate his solo music earnings to charity, the late Beatle's foundation continues to give hundreds of
articles.body: More than 50 years after George Harrison promised to donate his solo music earnings to charity, the late Beatle's foundation continues to give hundreds of thousands of pounds each year to causes around the world. Annual financial records filed with the Charity Commission for England and Wales show that the Material World Foundation spent £573,221 on charitable work during the 2024 reporting year. The money comes from an agreement Harrison made in 1973. He gave all publishing royalties from his hit solo album Living in the Material World to his newly created foundation permanently. Even decades after his death, income from record sales, streaming and radio play continues to support emergency relief, medical research and community arts projects around the world.Establishing a permanent giftHarrison founded the organisation in autumn 1973. He assigned the copyright income from nine tracks on his album Living in the Material World directly to the foundation. These included the publishing rights to his worldwide number-one single, Give Me Love (Give Me Peace on Earth). By handing over these rights permanently, Harrison ensured that money earned from sales, radio broadcasts and public performances of the songs would support charity rather than provide personal income. According to the official history on the Material World Foundation website, Harrison created the organisation to support unusual artistic projects, encourage alternative cultural education and provide financial help to established charities working with people with special needs. The foundation's first project, launched in late 1973, was to fund the Ravi Shankar Music Festival. The event brought leading Indian classical musicians to London to perform and record new compositions created by Shankar.Funding global humanitarian effortsOfficial records held by the Charity Commission show that the London-registered foundation operates independently and provides grants to charitable causes. It is managed by a board of four trustees, who receive no salary or other payment for their work. The financial reports explain how the foundation uses its income to fund projects directly. In 2024, it spent £573,221 on public health services, education programmes, emergency aid and environmental projects in the UK and other countries. Public records of its grants show that the foundation has supported medical organisations such as Médecins Sans Frontières, Great Ormond Street Hospital Children's Charity and Macmillan Cancer Support. It has also continued to fund groups working to protect children and young people, including the National Deaf Children's Society and the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC). When natural disasters or international emergencies occur, the trustees can direct extra funds towards relief work carried out by established non-governmental organisations. After Harrison died in November 2001, the foundation received further income from a special release of his 1970 hit single My Sweet Lord in early 2002. All net profits from the re-released CD single went directly into the foundation's main fund for distributing grants.Sustaining a musician's visionThe continuing income from Living in the Material World reflects the lasting popularity of Harrison's solo music. When Apple Records released the album in May 1973, it reached number one on the US Billboard chart and number two on the UK's Official Albums Chart. The album has remained popular through digital streaming services and physical anniversary editions. This has helped preserve the value of its copyright and provided the foundation with a steady source of money for charitable grants for more than five decades. The board of trustees, which includes Harrison's widow, Olivia Harrison, decides which organisations receive funding. The trustees do not receive salaries for their work. According to the governance arrangements described in the Charity Commission filings, keeping administrative costs low helps ensure that more of the royalty income reaches the charities and groups receiving support. The Material World Foundation continues to operate from its registered administrative base in London. Its future grant programmes will continue to draw on the royalties generated by Harrison's 1973 album and its songs, keeping his original charitable commitment alive decades after it was made.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2025, Lee and Don Cameron took a 12-month job as Low Isles’ live-in caretakers; their 7-day weeks start before 6 a.m. amid thousands of noisy birds
articles.summary: The Tasmanian couple took a 12-month contract as live-in caretakers of Low Island, part of the Great Barrier Reef, and traded a self-built off-grid home
articles.body: The Tasmanian couple took a 12-month contract as live-in caretakers of Low Island, part of the Great Barrier Reef, and traded a self-built off-grid home for a job that requires them to maintain buildings, manage vegetation and help protect the island’s natural environment. The couple’s appointment was announced by the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority on October 29, 2025, which said that they had won a tender to replace outgoing caretakers Colin and Renata Musson. The role involves looking after heritage buildings and infrastructure, coordinating with tour operators, welcoming visitors and monitoring compliance with marine park rules..The birds are part of the jobLow Island is about 15 kilometres northeast of Port Douglas, and along with nearby Woody Island, it forms the Low Isles group, a pair of coral cays that are surrounded by reef waters popular with snorkellers, researchers and tour groups. The area attracts about 50,000 visitors annually, according to the Marine Park Authority. The annual nesting season brought large numbers of bridled terns and pied imperial pigeons to the island, which is when the Camerons arrived, and in an October 28 report, ABC News described the noise from the birds as a constant feature of life there. Little terns tap along the island’s aluminium stairs, pigeons coo, and other seabirds produce louder calls through the night and early morning.Lee Cameron told ABC that she enjoyed observing the birds and their individual behaviour, even when the noise became difficult. The island’s wildlife is a part of the caretaking work, as the couple has experience with monitoring seabirds and other species through conservation volunteering in Tasmania.Maintenance without a nearby hardware storeCaretakers must clean and repair heritage buildings, manage weeds, keep visitor areas presentable and maintain essential infrastructure, while also overseeing systems that support the island’s off-grid operation, including solar power, rainwater collection and filtration, wastewater treatment and composting toilets. The Marine Park Authority describes Low Island as a carbon-neutral coral cay, and its facilities have to keep working despite the island’s isolation, heat, humidity and exposure to cyclones. Supplies and specialist help are not as readily available as they would be on the mainland, so caretakers need practical maintenance skills and the ability to handle problems independently.The Camerons spent 12 years travelling internationally by sailboat before returning to Tasmania, where they built an off-grid solar home overlooking the River Derwent. They had also volunteered on several remote islands and worked on heritage lighthouse projects, and their previous experience included conservation work on Maatsuyker Island, where volunteers monitor wildlife in challenging conditions. The couple’s Low Isles contract also requires them to welcome visitors and liaise with tour operators, which means that the island is both a workplace and a destination used by day-trippers, even though the caretakers live there full-time.A seven-day working weekABC News reported that the typical day begins before 6 a.m. and that the work continues seven days a week. Tasks vary, but can include raking, checking facilities, gardening, repairs and cleaning, and Lee said that the routine involved more walking than she had expected when she first saw the size of the island. The couple have a residence on Low Island, while separate accommodation is available for visiting researchers and volunteers. They can seek help with larger jobs that exceed what two caretakers can manage themselves, but ordinary upkeep remains their responsibility.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: “More money, more families”: How sports couple Allie LaForce and Joe Smith turned a charity gala into $600,000 for Huntington’s disease families
articles.summary: Sports broadcaster Allie LaForce and MLB pitcher Joe Smith held a successful charity gala in Houston, raising $600,000 for families affected by Huntington's disease, with efforts focused on fertility treatment and research support.
articles.body: Allie LaForce summed up the purpose of the HelpCureHD gala with the words, “More money, more families. That simple,” as she described her goal of raising $1 million at the next event after the 2023 gala raised a record $600,000 for Huntington’s disease research and fertility treatment support, according to CultureMap Houston.The sports broadcaster, along with former Major League Baseball pitcher Joe Smith, directed attention and funding toward families affected by Huntington’s disease. The annual event brings together professional athletes, donors, medical specialists, and families who have received help from the couple’s foundation, which supports research and helps eligible families access fertility treatments that are designed to prevent the inherited disease from passing to their children.The September 2023 gala took place at Union Station inside Minute Maid Park, which was home of the Houston Astros at the time. CultureMap Houston reported that the event raised a record $600,000, with Astros players, team owner Jim Crane and other guests attending. The evening included a dinner, a silent auction, and donated experiences and memorabilia.A family diagnosis shaped the foundationSmith and LaForce established HelpCureHD in 2017, and their work started with Smith’s mother being diagnosed with Huntington’s disease in 2012 and dying in August 2020 after an eight-year battle with the condition, which his grandmother also died from. Huntington’s disease is an inherited disorder that progressively damages nerve cells in the brain and can affect movement, thinking and behaviour. A person who has a parent with the disease has a 50% chance of inheriting the genetic variant responsible for it. Smith has said publicly that he has chosen not to undergo genetic testing, instead focusing their efforts on helping families who want children without the disease. Their experience with the condition made fertility assistance a central part of the foundation’s work.A 2021 report by the Houston Chronicle described how the couple launched HelpCureHD to provide financial and emotional support to patients and families, as well as help cover the costs of fertility treatment. It also documented their own experience with preimplantation genetic testing and in-vitro fertilisation.How the money helps familiesHelpCureHD provides grants to eligible families pursuing preimplantation genetic testing with in-vitro fertilisation, commonly called PGT-IVF. The process allows embryos created through IVF to be tested for a specific genetic variant before an embryo is selected for transfer, and for families at risk of passing on Huntington’s disease, the approach can help them have a child who does not carry the disease-causing variant. The treatment can be expensive and may require more than one IVF cycle, and the foundation’s financial assistance is intended to reduce that barrier for families who might otherwise struggle to afford the process. The charity also supports efforts to raise awareness and fund work related to Huntington’s disease.The organisation’s public updates describe the foundation’s focus on helping families pursue fertility treatment and supporting efforts to combat the disease. Research may contribute to better treatments or, eventually, a cure, but the foundation’s IVF grants address a more immediate concern for families who want to reduce the chance of passing the disease to their children. Genetic testing does not treat Huntington’s disease in an affected person; it is used in this context to inform embryo selection during fertility treatment.A gala built around families, not just donorsThe 2023 event also gave families who had received assistance an opportunity to meet the donors and supporters behind the programme, with CultureMap reporting that the couple had helped more than 135 couples pursue the goal of having a child free of Huntington’s disease. Their young son, Jacob, who was born in November 2022, also attended the gala. LaForce has spoken about the physical and emotional demands of IVF, including the repeated procedures involved in fertility treatment, and the couple’s public advocacy has drawn attention to the choices faced by people who have a family history of an inherited disorder and want biological children.The gala’s $600,000 total was a fundraising result for that year’s event, not an annual guarantee or a measure of the foundation’s full lifetime funding. The couple has continued to organise fundraising events and promote HelpCureHD’s work through their sports and philanthropic networks. The foundation’s model depends on contributions from donors and supporters to help eligible families meet fertility costs, and for those families, the assistance can make a costly medical process more accessible while they weigh the personal decisions that come with a hereditary diagnosis.You use AI every day. articles.title: After 54 years of marriage, a Kentucky widow rejected her husband's will to claim more of his estate; his children from a prior marriage challenged her mental capacity, but an October 23 court halted the probate inquiry
articles.summary: A Kentucky appeals court has stopped a lower court from investigating the mental capacity of Tamara Williams, a widow who rejected her late husband's will
articles.body: A Kentucky appeals court has stopped a lower court from investigating the mental capacity of Tamara Williams, a widow who rejected her late husband's will to claim a larger share of his estate. The appeals court ruled that district courts do not have the legal authority to handle disputed family cases of this kind. On 23 October 2026, the Kentucky Court of Appeals issued a writ of prohibition ordering the Montgomery District Court to stop all proceedings into Tamara's mental state. The judges unanimously ruled that the district court had acted beyond its legal powers. They said disputed claims involving undue influence and mental incapacity must be heard in circuit court. The decision follows a dispute over the estate of Julian D. Williams, who died in February 2023. He left behind a substantial estate and a will naming his two adult children from an earlier marriage, Jeffrey C. Williams and Leslie A. Williams, as co-executors.Renouncing the will for statutory shareUnder Julian's will, his assets were placed in a trust. The income from the trust was to be divided equally among three beneficiaries, his wife of 54 years, Tamara, and his two adult children. After Tamara's death, the remaining money and assets held in the trust were to pass entirely to Jeffrey and Leslie. In November 2023, Tamara used her legal right under Kentucky law to reject her husband's will. By choosing the share of the estate guaranteed to a surviving spouse by state law instead of accepting the trust arrangements, she stood to receive a much larger part of the estate directly. Three months later, Jeffrey and Leslie filed a motion in district court asking for Tamara's decision to be overturned. They brought the challenge as individual beneficiaries, rather than in their roles as estate co-executors. The stepchildren claimed that Tamara did not have the mental capacity to understand the decision she had made. They also alleged that her nephew and niece had improperly influenced her. Both relatives held power of attorney for Tamara. Tamara challenged their claims. She maintained that she was mentally capable of making her own decisions and had clearly exercised a right available to surviving spouses under Kentucky law.District court orders discoveryAlthough the stepchildren's original motion did not include medical evidence to support their claims, the Montgomery District Court allowed both sides to investigate Tamara's mental health. The parties exchanged written questions and documents, submitted sworn statements and took depositions. In September 2025, the district court rejected Tamara's request to distribute the estate according to her decision to claim a spousal share. The court refused the stepchildren's request to make Tamara undergo an independent medical examination. However, it ordered her to attend a formal deposition, where she would have to answer questions under oath. Tamara sought to stop the deposition and prevent further investigation into her mental state. She asked the Montgomery Circuit Court to issue a writ of prohibition, arguing that the district court was handling a complex legal dispute beyond its limited authority over probate matters. Special Judge Eddy Coleman of the Montgomery Circuit Court rejected her request. He concluded that earlier court decisions required him to recognise district courts' authority over routine probate cases. Tamara then appealed his decision to the state's intermediate appeals court.Appeals panel steps inThe Kentucky Court of Appeals overturned the circuit court's decision. It found that the district court had gone beyond its legal powers by trying to resolve a disputed case about Tamara's mental capacity. Writing for the appeals panel, Judge Glenn E. Acree explained that district courts can deal with routine probate matters when there is no dispute. However, Kentucky law reserves contested cases involving opposing parties for circuit courts. The judges stressed that trying to cancel a legal decision that someone has already made, based on claims that the person lacked mental capacity, is a disputed legal matter that must be handled by a circuit court. "We conclude the district court is adjudicating an adversary proceeding without subject matter jurisdiction," Judge Acree wrote in the official opinion. The court also noted that people who sign legal documents are presumed to have the mental capacity to do so unless a court with the proper authority determines otherwise. The appeals panel further found that the stepchildren had tried to challenge Tamara's decision after the fact without first filing a proper civil lawsuit in circuit court. The ruling sends the case back to the Montgomery Circuit Court, which must issue a formal order directing the district court to stop its investigation into Tamara's mental capacity. This allows Tamara's decision to claim her statutory share of the estate to move forward unless Jeffrey and Leslie begin a separate civil lawsuit in circuit court to challenge it.You use AI every day. articles.title: Trump gears up for Iran escalation after US polls
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has hinted that his forces in the Mideast would resume strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections on Nov 3.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has hinted that his forces in the Mideast would resume strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections on Nov 3. The President has already sent a third aircraft carrier strike group and 10,000 additional sailors and Marines toward the Persian Gulf to give US commanders more options if he restarts hostilities.Last week, defence secretary Pete Hegseth also made an unannounced stop in Israel — which launched the war against Iran alongside the US — where he met with PM Benjamin Netanyahu just days ahead of the Israeli leader’s sensitive re-election bid. Staffing at Middle Eastern bases, which have been hit hard by Iranian counterstrikes, has reportedly been reduced.The US State Department this week ordered the departure of some diplomats and families in Saudi Arabia, following the Iran-backed Houthis expanding the conflict into Saudi Arabia. Houthis have pummelled the Riyadh airport and energy facilities with drones and missiles, killing dozens and wounding hundreds.Against that backdrop, Iran is bracing for a fresh US bombing campaign around midterms and is preparing to retaliate across West Asia, including against Israel and UAE, according to a person familiar with Tehran’s thinking. The period between the US polls and when the new Congress takes office in Jan will be the most difficult period.Resumption of war won’t change Tehran’s position, says Iran ministerThe only way out of the current conflict is a deal that allows both sides to claim a win, Iranian minister said.Iran’s foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that a potential resumption of war with Israel and the US would not change his country’s positions. “Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same,” said Araghchi during a televised event in Tehran. “They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past.”Some Gulf-state officials have a high degree of confidence that violence will resume, and said they fear it could be worse than before the pause, according to a person familiar with the UAE govt’s thinking. “We’ve knocked the hell out of them — and we may do it a little bit further,” Trump told reporters Thursday, echoing that sentiment.Meanwhile, Iran is attacking more ships in or near the Strait of Hormuz — and causing more severe damage — than earlier in the conflict as it deploys guided missiles rather than attack drones, according to shipping and maritime security officials.Renewed fighting could help Netanyahu force political rivals into a national unity govt, while strikes could help Trump project a “dramatic show of force to project strength at home”, according to International Crisis Group Mideast expert Ali Vaez. “Both Trump and Netanyahu may see war with Iran as a political escape hatch,” Vaez said. “But both risk discovering that a war intended to rescue their political fortunes could end up burying them.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Signals, markings not ready, Vyapar Kendra road in Gurgaon chokes as motorists shift to two-way traffic
articles.summary: Gurgaon’s Vyapar Kendra road sees heavy congestion as motorists start two-way traffic before official rollout; GMDA says signals, markings and bollards still pending.
articles.body: Gurgaon: Motorists have started using Vyapar Kendra road in both directions despite the stretch not being officially opened to two-way traffic, leading to confusion and congestion over the past few days. Median bollards are still being installed and traffic signals are being modified to accommodate the proposed change.GMDA said the road was still meant to operate as a one-way stretch and that two-way movement would begin only after the remaining infrastructure work was completed and traffic police formally implemented the change.“The median installation and other finishing work are underway. The traffic signals were originally installed according to the one-way arrangement and are now being modified to regulate traffic in both directions. Once the infrastructure is ready, we will inform the traffic police, who will implement the revised two-way movement. Until then, the existing one-way system is supposed to remain in force,” a GMDA official said.The remaining work includes installing flexible spring bollards along the median, thermoplastic road markings and other road safety features, the official added.However, motorists have already begun travelling in both directions, creating conflict points particularly near the market and adjoining residential areas. Residents said a journey of less than 2km was taking up to 30 minutes, compared with two to three minutes earlier. They added that the absence of traffic personnel had worsened the confusion.“The situation has become particularly difficult over the past few days. There is no traffic police personnel on the ground to monitor the situation or manage the movement of vehicles. Commuters are left to figure out which side to take, and this is leading to confusion and congestion,” said Veenu Pasricha, a resident of Sushant Lok-1.Pasricha said the dividers had narrowed the carriageway at the beginning of the stretch, forcing vehicles into two lanes and creating a bottleneck. Vehicles entering or exiting Vyapar Kendra market and those travelling towards Sushant Lok also have to navigate the same stretch, increasing the risk of traffic conflicts.“There is no proper arrangement for vehicles entering the residential areas or the market, or for those exiting the market and joining the main road. There are no clearly defined cuts or designated turning points to guide motorists. As a result, vehicles bunch up at the same point, and people are unsure which direction to take,” Pasricha said.Residents called for better coordination between GMDA and traffic police, clearly marked entry and exit points, action against encroachments and deployment of traffic personnel at key junctions.Sudhir Sachdeva, another resident, said roadside vendors and weak enforcement of traffic rules had compounded the problem. He added that pedestrians had limited access to the footpaths constructed along the stretch.“Traffic congestion has increased after the road was made two-way, even when there is no formal implementation. When you put the bollards, people start using it as a two-way road. There should be proper information displays on the road to avoid confusion. At the same time, vendors occupy space along the road. The authorities must first enforce the rules strictly and ensure that vendors do not obstruct traffic,” Sachdeva said.A similar situation prevails on Galleria Market road, where roadside parking and encroachments have reduced the usable carriageway. Residents fear congestion could worsen during peak hours if two-way traffic is allowed before these issues are not addressed.Narender Mehta, general secretary of the Sector 43 RWA, raised concerns over the use of flexible plastic posts along the central median, saying they might not provide adequate protection against vehicles crossing into the opposite lane.“A central verge should provide effective physical and visual separation between traffic moving in opposite directions and help reduce the risk of head-on collisions. Given the instances of overspeeding, reckless overtaking and drunk driving, particularly at night, flexible posts may not offer adequate protection if a vehicle crosses into the opposite lane. The design needs to be carefully reviewed to ensure commuter safety,” Mehta said.GMDA began revamping Galleria Market road and Vyapar Kendra road in 2024 to facilitate the restoration of two-way traffic. The parallel stretches had operated as one-way roads for around 11 years, with the arrangement introduced to ease congestion.The redevelopment included widening and strengthening the roads, improving footpaths, developing cycle tracks and landscaping. The project was scheduled for completion within 12 months but missed several deadlines.GMDA spent around Rs 21.7 crore on the revamp of Galleria Market road and Rs 22.4 crore on Vyapar Kendra road, taking the combined project cost to approximately Rs 44.1 crore.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Gurgaon | Silver Rate in Gurgaon | Bank Holidays in Gurgaon | Public Holidays in Gurgaon | Gurgaon AQI | Weather in Gurgaon | Petrol Price in Gurgaon | Diesel Price in Gurgaon | CNG Price in Gurgaon | LPG Price in GurgaonStay updated with the latest Gurgaon news. articles.title: Haryana cities breached annual PM10 limit every year since 2019
articles.summary: CPCB/CREA data shows Haryana cities breached annual PM10 limits every year since 2019; 2025 peaked with Dharuhera worst-hit and major monitoring gaps.
articles.body: Gurgaon: None of Haryana’s monitored cities has met India’s annual PM10 standard every year since 2019, according to Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data shared by Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).All 178 PM10 readings recorded across the state between Jan 1, 2019 and Oct 23, 2026, exceeded the annual limit of 60 micrograms per cubic metre (µg/m³). The lowest reading, 72.7 µg/m³ in Mandikhera in 2026, was still above the prescribed standard. Around 88% of the readings, or 156 entries, also crossed 100 µg/m³, the national 24-hour limit.“The fact that all cities in Haryana have exceeded the annual PM10 standard for five consecutive years points to a systemic pollution problem. Haryana needs a state-level mitigation strategy that tackles pollution sources across urban, peri-urban and rural areas, rather than relying primarily on city-specific action plans. The next phase of National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) must expand its coverage in Haryana, as Faridabad is currently the only city in Haryana included under the programme. A coordinated regional approach is essential to achieve consistent reductions in pollution,” said Manoj Kumar, air analyst, CREA.PM10 concentrations peaked in 2025. Across 22 cities with data for both 2024 and 2025, the average level rose from 119.9 µg/m³ to 175.2 µg/m³. Dharuhera recorded the highest annual concentration at 277.8 µg/m³, followed by Bahadurgarh at 263.9 µg/m³, Sonipat at 235.4 µg/m³, Panipat at 229.3 µg/m³ and Ballabgarh at 223.4 µg/m³. Six cities reported levels above 200 µg/m³ that year.The data indicate that particulate pollution has remained high across Haryana, though city-level trends vary. In Gurgaon, the annual PM10 average declined from 190.2 µg/m³ in 2019 to 148.4 µg/m³ in 2020. It then rose to 174.5 µg/m³ in 2021 and peaked at 196.7 µg/m³ in 2022. The level fell to 176 µg/m³ in 2023, increased to 185.6 µg/m³ in 2024 and declined again to 159.6 µg/m³ in 2025.Despite the fall in 2025, Gurgaon’s PM10 level remained more than 2.6 times the national annual standard. The city’s available average for 2026 stood at 164.9 µg/m³ till Oct 23.Other cities also showed sharp variations. Ballabgarh recorded 226.0 µg/m³ in 2019 and 223.4 µg/m³ in 2025. Panipat’s average declined from 187.3 µg/m³ in 2019 to 108.2 µg/m³ in 2024, before rising steeply to 229.3 µg/m³ in 2025. Sonipat recorded 155.5 µg/m³ in 2019, 125.5 µg/m³ in 2024 and 235.4 µg/m³ in 2025.The 2026 figures show that PM10 pollution remains elevated in several areas. Among the 24 cities with available data, Ballabgarh recorded the highest average at 195.1 µg/m³, followed by Gurgaon at 164.9 µg/m³, Panipat at 164.2 µg/m³ and Faridabad at 144.1 µg/m³. Sixteen of the 24 cities reported concentrations above 100 µg/m³.The 2026 data covers only the period till Oct 23 and cannot be directly compared with full-year averages. Nov and Dec, when pollution levels typically rise, are not included.The dataset also highlights gaps in Haryana’s air quality monitoring network. A note accompanying the data says that, except for Gurgaon and Panchgaon, the listed cities had less than 75% valid PM10 data because continuous ambient air quality monitoring stations were not operating. Rohtak and Panchgaon have data only from 2025.These monitoring gaps call for caution while interpreting year-on-year changes, including the sharp rise recorded in 2025. articles.title: Update real-time medicine stock info on online portal, govt hospitals across Haryana told
articles.summary: Haryana health dept tells govt hospitals to update online drug portal in real time and match physical stock, warning action for discrepancies; HMSCL orders biometric access.
articles.body: Gurgaon: Haryana’s health department has directed civil surgeons across the state to ensure regular updates of medicine procurement, availability and consumption records on the online drug management portal, warning that discrepancies between recorded and physical stocks will invite accountability.The directions require govt hospitals and other healthcare institutions to enter details of medicines procured locally into the portal and update records of purchases, availability and consumption promptly. The Essential Drug List (EDL) will be used to monitor medicine availability, with officials asked to ensure that online records match the physical stock.Responsibility will be fixed for discrepancies between portal entries and actual stocks, and officials and employees found responsible for lapses could face action. Healthcare institutions have also been directed to regularly verify medicine stocks and monitor their consumption.The department has stressed the need to ensure that medicines available through the govt supply system are prescribed to patients. Doctors will be encouraged to prescribe available govt-supplied medicines to help patients avoid unnecessary inconvenience.Separately, the Haryana Medical Services Corporation Limited (HMSCL) has directed measures to prevent unauthorised access to staff cabins and areas where sensitive files and procurement-related documents are kept.HMSCL managing director Dr Manoj Kumar issued instructions for installing biometric access control gates in staff areas to regulate entry. Outsiders will not be allowed to enter staff cabins without authorisation.Biometric attendance has been made mandatory for officers and employees, who will be required to record their attendance through the system. Visitors will have to enter their details in a designated register and wait in designated areas. Meetings with staff will have to follow the prescribed procedure, with visitors barred from accessing restricted areas without authorisation.The instructions are aimed at safeguarding sensitive documents and ensuring that access to staff areas is regulated. articles.title: Painter Jogen Chowdhury, master of line on canvas and paper, passes away
articles.summary: Painter Jogen Chowdhury dies at 87 in Kolkata after rare blood cancer; acclaimed for fluid line work, human frailty themes, and mentoring emerging artists.
articles.body: Kolkata: Painter Jogen Chowdhury, hailed as a master of line both on canvas and on paper and celebrated for his portrayal of human frailty, died at a city hospital on Sunday, leaving behind an unmatched legacy in contemporary Indian art.Beyond his distinctive visual language and pioneering aesthetics, the 87-year-old creator of ‘Day Dreaming', ‘Tiger In The Moonlit Night’, ‘Reminiscences of a Dream’, ‘Moonstruck’, ‘The Wound’, ‘Mona Lisa in my Dream’, ‘Her Silver Throne’ and ‘The Blue Sari’ will also be remembered for mentoring and supporting emerging artists.Chowdhury, who was professor emeritus at Kala Bhavana in Visva-Bharati, passed away after battling a rare type of blood cancer for 14 months. Paying his respects to the artist, CM Suvendu Adhikari described Chowdhury as a “maestro whose distinctive strokes redefined Indian modern art” and “a towering pillar of our cultural world” whose contributions brought global recognition to Bengal.Chowdhury’s canvases were characterised by his mastery of the continuous, fluid line — unbroken strokes that defined the psychological character of his subjects and reshaped the human form. His linear precision served the primacy of the silent human figure, which remained the central focus and was often set against white backgrounds devoid of specific environments so the body could communicate in silence.“There was tremendous power in his sharp lines that sometimes even seem to penetrate the surface of the canvas. The lines embody a linearly defined space and that space is often attacked and assaulted by a scar or a thrust. In the process, the precarity of the space is underscored,” said Samik Bandyopadhyay, teacher, publisher, writer, translator and art commentator.Through an expressionist style, creative X-ray vision, and signature distortion, his subjects emerged as caricatures with imaginary faces that conveyed authentic psychological traits through a tension between the known and the unknown. These technical choices articulated deep expressions of isolation, functioning as a potent social commentary that blended reality with imagination to reflect collective human consciousness while rejecting monolithic notions of Indianness and rigid traditions.Partition left an impact on his life. “It deeply influenced his perception of interpersonal relations, love, cruelty and hatred, forming the root of his lifelong exploration of the grotesque as an extension of the inner world,” said art scholar Pranab Ranjan Ray.Born in Bangladesh’s Faridpur in 1939, Chowdhury graduated from Government College of Art & Craft in 1960. In 1965, backed by a scholarship and with a crowd-funded ship ticket to Paris priced Rs 800, Chowdhury arrived at École nationale supérieure des beaux-arts. “During his time there, he crossed paths with Jimi Hendrix and sketched his portrait, delighting the legendary musician so much that Hendrix signed and penned a compliment on it,” said artist Hiran Mitra.Following his return from France, Chowdhury joined Handloom Board in Chennai before serving as Keeper of Art at Rashtrapati Bhavan from 1972 to 1987.“It was during this time that an interrupted presidential portrait session — halted by a forgotten pair of dentures — sparked a profound realisation about human fragility without bone and teeth. This became his central thought for a series he did on politicians,” Mitra said. Decades later, when he returned to the corridors of power as a Trinamool Congress Rajya Sabha MP, his sketchbook was never far: he drew portraits of personalities such as Manmohan Singh, Sitaram Yechury and Smriti Irani, among others.He also remained dedicated to nurturing others — supporting students at Santiniketan by buying their work and ultimately establishing Jogen Chowdhury Centre for Arts in Kolkata in 2019. “He promoted many at Gallery Charubasona (part of Jogen Chowdhury Centre) in Lake Gardens and even helped some newcomers financially, too,” Mitra said.Culturist Sundeep Bhutoria remembers Chowdhury as the man with a small camera in his pocket, “forever capturing candid moments of fellow artistes”. Bangladesh revered him as a living bridge of undivided Bengal, he said.Not many know that Chowdhury possessed a gift for poetry and prose. “Nobody has ever tried to link his poetry to his works. I think it is worth exploring,” Bandyopadhyay said. In 1998, he wrote “Bhalobashar Katha” — a four-line poem reflecting on how matters of the heart, though timeless and ancient, remain eternally fresh and impossible to live without.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kolkata | Silver Rate in Kolkata | Bank Holidays in Kolkata | Public Holidays in Kolkata | Kolkata AQI | Weather in Kolkata | Petrol Price in Kolkata | Diesel Price in Kolkata | CNG Price in Kolkata | LPG Price in KolkataStay updated with the latest Kolkata news. articles.summary: YEIDA issues LoI to Motherson for 150-acre automotive parts plant in Noida; Rs 3,491 crore investment, 20,000 jobs in 5 years; final allotment awaited.
articles.body: Noida: Yamuna Expressway Industrial Development Authority (YEIDA) has issued a letter of intent (LoI) to Samvardhana Motherson International Ltd (SAMIL) to set up an automotive components manufacturing facility across 150 acres in sectors 6 and 7. The company plans to invest Rs 3,491 crore in the facility, which is expected to generate around 20,000 jobs over the next five years.YEIDA CEO RK Singh said that the formal allotment letter is expected to be issued by the state govt in the coming days.SAMIL, part of the Motherson Group, is a global manufacturer and supplier of automotive components, providing design, engineering, manufacturing, assembly and logistics solutions.The proposed facility will manufacture a wide range of automotive components, including wiring harnesses, PVC-insulated wires, outer rear-view mirrors, interior and exterior mirror systems, automotive lighting systems and exhaust systems. It will also undertake the manufacturing of cutting tools, aerospace components, injection-moulded products and advanced tooling solutions.Officials said the facility will be developed as an integrated manufacturing complex, bringing together various stages of production under one roof. It will have infrastructure for design support, precision tooling, component manufacturing, sub-assembly, final assembly and product testing. It is expected to streamline manufacturing operations, improve production efficiency and strengthen the automotive component supply chain in the region.Since commercial operations began at Noida International Airport in June this year, the Yamuna Expressway region has witnessed growing investor interest and industrial activity. The airport’s operationalisation has strengthened the region’s appeal as an investment destination, with several companies proposing to establish manufacturing units, logistics facilities and other industrial projects along the Yamuna Expressway, officials said.Last month, the Authority reviewed the progress of industrial plots measuring more than 4,000 sqm. Of the 295 such plots, lease deeds have been executed for 181, possession has been given for 152 and construction has started on 69. Production has commenced at 13 units.In Sector 28’s Medical Device Park, 123 of the 203 plots have been allotted, while possession has been given for 75 plots and construction has started on 28.In neighbouring Sector 29, 159 plots have been allotted in the Apparel Park, while 503 plots have been allotted in the MSME Park and 188 in the Handicraft Park.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Noida | Silver Rate in Noida | Bank Holidays in Noida | Public Holidays in Noida | Noida AQI | Weather in Noida | Petrol Price in Noida | Diesel Price in Noida | CNG Price in Noida | LPG Price in NoidaStay updated with the latest Noida news. articles.title: BJP calls protest over Kharge’s ‘baap’ remark
articles.summary: PATNA/NEW DELHI: Congress party president Mallikarjun Kharge’s remark about PM Narendra Modi’s father raised a furore in BJP on Sunday, with the party
articles.body: PATNA/NEW DELHI: Congress party president Mallikarjun Kharge’s remark about PM Narendra Modi’s father raised a furore in BJP on Sunday, with the party announcing a nationwide protest on Monday against Kharge’s “indecent and offensive” remarks.Addressing a gathering at Bapu Sabhagar in Patna, Kharge was interrupted by a young member of the audience who shouted “Modi nahin jayega (Modi will not go)”. The Congress chief shot back, saying, “Modi ka baap bhi jayega (Modi’s father, too, will have to go)”.The youth was removed from the venue by the organisers of the function marking the 139th birth anniversary of Bihar’s first chief minister Shri Krishna Sinha.Union home minister Amit Shah targeted Congress for its frequent personal attacks on Modi and blamed it on simmering frustration within the party over its continuous poll losses over the last 12 years.Not the first time Cong has abused Modi or his family, says Shah"Kharge has broken all norms of decency by commenting on Modi’s father,” Shah said, adding Congress was frequently crossing the limits of decency under Rahul Gandhi. “This is not the first time Congress has abused Modi or his family,” he said, recalling barbs like “maut ka saudagar” for him and abusive reference to his mother.BJP announced the protests against Congress after an organisational meeting, which was presided over by party chief Nitin Nabin and Shah. Nabin said a certain decorum was expected of the political opposition but it had now become a trend for Rahul and the entire opposition to drag dead family members in their speeches. BJP MP Dharmendra Pradhan said, “Having forgotten the bounds of propriety in political opposition, Congress is now resorting solely to personal insults.”Stepping up his attack on BJP over Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, Kharge described the ongoing protests against the exercise as the “second war for independence”.“If people have no voting rights, the country will be enslaved. It (the protests) is the second war for independence. We will have to fight for our vote, voting rights, for democracy and to save the Constitution,” Kharge said, demanding the rollback of SIR and the use of ballot papers in elections. articles.title: 5 held for stealing 6 tonnes of iron rods from construction sites across NCR
articles.summary: Five arrested for stealing 6 tonnes of iron rods from 16 NCR construction sites in a month; gang leader shot in leg during police encounter, scrap dealer held.
articles.body: Noida: Five persons were arrested for allegedly stealing over six tonnes of iron rods from 16 construction sites across NCR in a month and selling them to a scrap dealer in Ghaziabad. The gang leader, police said, was shot in the leg during an exchange of fire.The accused were identified as Raju Singh alias Raja (34), Rahul Singh (30), Arjun Kumar (27) and Sunil Kumar (20), all residents of Delhi, and Shabbir (45), a scrap dealer from Ghaziabad.Abhay Kumar Mishra, Noida ADCP, said a team from Sector 58 police station was checking vehicles at Jaipuriya junction in Sector 62 on Saturday night when it tried to stop Raju and Rahul, who were riding an Apache bike. The duo allegedly sped towards D Park. Their motorcycle skidded on a bend, causing the two to fall off it. Police said they then opened fire at the team, prompting retaliatory firing in which Raju was shot in the leg. He was taken to a hospital, while Rahul was arrested.Police recovered Rs 2,500 in cash from them, a country-made .315-bore pistol, a live cartridge and an empty cartridge from the duo. The motorcycle they were riding was stolen from Sector 20 a few months ago, and an FIR had been registered there.During questioning, Rahul allegedly named Arjun and Sunil, who were waiting behind D Park with a scooter. They were subsequently arrested from Khoda Road.“During questioning, the accused said they conducted recces before stealing iron rods from construction sites and selling them to a scrap dealer in Ghaziabad,” Mishra said. Police recovered two quintals of rods from Shabbir’s possession.Mishra said Raju was the gang leader and had more than a dozen cases registered against him across NCR. articles.title: Pink headlined a San Diego concert that raised $8.25 million for cancer research; the benefit series has now generated more than $28 million across four star-powered events
articles.summary: A concert featuring American singer Pink in San Diego has raised $8.25 million for cancer research, taking the total collected through the Concert for
articles.body: A concert featuring American singer Pink in San Diego has raised $8.25 million for cancer research, taking the total collected through the Concert for Cures series to more than $28 million. Around 25,000 people attended the May 15 event at Petco Park, including thousands of cancer survivors. The fundraising figures were announced by Curebound, a San Diego-based organisation that supports research on cancer.The concert brought together music fans, cancer survivors and organisations supporting medical research. The event was organised to raise money for studies focused on preventing cancer, detecting it earlier and improving treatment options.Pink was the main performer at this year's concert. Her performance included several of her well-known songs, along with aerial acts that are a regular feature of her live shows. She also spoke about the importance of the organisation's work and thanked those who had gathered to support it.“I was part of some of the most important work that there is to do. Cancer sucks, and I am just very grateful to be of use, and I am very grateful to be here with all of you, and I am just very grateful,” Pink told the audience, as quoted by the Times of San Diego.The $8.25 million raised during the evening was another contribution to a fundraising programme that has been running since 2022. Over four concerts, the initiative has brought together more than 60,000 attendees, with performances by some of the biggest names in international music.Concerts brought more than $28 millionPink is the latest musician to take part in Concert for Cures, which has previously featured Elton John, Ed Sheeran and Alicia Keys. The artists performed at different venues in San Diego, helping Curebound reach audiences beyond the medical and research communities.Elton John performed at Petco Park, while Alicia Keys appeared alongside the San Diego Symphony Orchestra. Ed Sheeran's concert took place at the Rady Shell at Jacobs Park, where he performed before a sold-out audience.The organisation's CEO, Robin Toft, addressed the audience during Pink's concert and explained why public contributions were particularly important at a time of uncertainty over national research funding.According to Curebound CEO Robin Toft, the contributions made by those attending the concert would help fund research into better ways to prevent, detect and treat cancer. She also stressed the importance of such fundraising efforts at a time when national funding for scientific research remained uncertain.How the money will be usedCurebound funds scientific projects examining different aspects of cancer, including how the disease develops, how it can be identified and how patients can be treated. Its work covers cancers affecting both adults and children.The organisation has so far awarded $51.5 million in research grants, supporting 170 studies involving 23 types of cancer.The funding has also contributed to 28 clinical trials. Clinical trials involve testing medical treatments or other interventions in people to assess their safety and effectiveness.Another result of the organisation's investments has been the additional funding secured for research. Curebound reported that projects it supported had attracted $161 million in follow-on funding, allowing scientists to expand their work beyond the initial grants.Rick Valencia, chair of Curebound's board, said the organisation was focused on what scientific progress could mean for patients and their families. Valencia co-chaired the 2026 concert organising committee with his daughter, Aubrey Salvati.According to Curebound Board Chair Rick Valencia, progress in cancer research could give patients and their families more treatment options and more time together. articles.title: In 2025, a Delaware couple planned a 24-by-28-foot garage, but their HOA rejected its metal siding and roof and recorded a violation against their property; a court magistrate has now ruled the notice must be cancelled
articles.summary: A Delaware couple who faced legal action from their homeowners association over plans to build a detached garage have won their court case.
articles.body: A Delaware couple who faced legal action from their homeowners association over plans to build a detached garage have won their court case. A judicial magistrate ordered the cancellation of a recorded violation notice against their property. Magistrate in Chancery Selena E. Molina ruled that the community's board had gone beyond its authority when it rejected the couple's proposed building materials and placed a legal claim against their property's title. The decision allows the couple to move ahead with building their 24-by-28-foot garage without facing fines or other legal restrictions linked to the dispute. The case was heard in the Delaware Court of Chancery and involved homeowners John and Sandra Mitchell and the board of directors of their residential community.Clash over building materialsThe dispute began in 2025 when the couple submitted plans to their homeowners association to build a detached garage measuring 24 by 28 feet on their property. Their design included metal siding and a metal roof, chosen to match other smaller buildings on neighbouring properties. The board rejected the plans, claiming that the community's property rules banned metal exterior finishes. It argued that detached buildings had to use traditional vinyl siding and asphalt shingles instead. The homeowners challenged the decision. They pointed out that several other properties in the development already had metal roofs and detached storage sheds. Despite their objections, the board took further action. Its directors filed a formal notice of violation against the couple's property in the county land records. This created a legal issue with the property's title, potentially making it harder for the couple to sell or refinance their home without first resolving the alleged violation. The couple then filed a lawsuit in the Delaware Court of Chancery. They asked the court to overturn the board's decision and remove the violation notice from the public land records.Arbitrary enforcement of covenantsIn a detailed judicial report released by the Delaware Court of Chancery, Magistrate Molina reviewed the community's founding documents and its past decisions on similar building projects. The court found that the association had general authority to review changes to buildings and other structures. However, the written property restrictions did not clearly ban metal siding or metal roofing on detached buildings. Magistrate Molina also pointed out that the board had allowed similar buildings with metal siding and metal roof features on other properties in the same development over the years. Under Delaware property law, homeowners associations cannot apply unwritten design rules selectively or arbitrarily. They must follow the restrictions set out in their governing documents. The court also explained that property restrictions must be interpreted in favour of the owner's right to use their land freely. If the community's rules are unclear, the uncertainty must be resolved in favour of the property owner rather than the association.Ordering the cancellation of the violation noticeMagistrate Molina recommended a final judgment in favour of the homeowners. She directed the county recorder of deeds to remove the violation notice from the public records. The magistrate also declared that the association's original rejection of the couple's 24-by-28-foot garage plans was legally invalid. Under the ruling, the board cannot take further enforcement action or impose fines against John and Sandra Mitchell because they chose metal siding and roofing materials. Lawyers who advise homeowners associations in Delaware have followed the case as part of a wider body of legal decisions concerning disputes over residential property rules. The Court of Chancery's ruling reinforces the need for housing associations to maintain clear, written standards before limiting changes homeowners can make to their properties. It also places limits on the use of recorded claims against property titles during disputes over alleged rule violations. For the Mitchells, the decision removes the recorded violation and clears a major legal obstacle to their proposed garage.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
